<reason>Both sides were sharp, but CON (A) won the two decisive exchanges. First, A's core charge — that every PRO success story (Maya Bay, Fjaðrárgljúfur, Angels Landing) recovered via capacity tools, not geotag limits — was never squarely answered; when A's Q2 demanded one site where promotion limits alone worked, B called the question "rigged" and fell back on Amsterdam, which A persuasively reclassified as a destination controlling its own speech. Second, A caught B's scope shift from "commercial-scale promotion" [B2.7] to "yes, it reaches the selfie" [B4.2] and converted it into a broader-but-weaker indictment: a voluntary request to Meta that reaches ordinary posts yet can't be enforced or verified. B's "both, not either" framing and tag-not-tagger distinction were genuinely strong, but A explicitly adapted to the complement frame in R1 and then carried the "what does it add" burden. A also answered B's best pressure (gateless sites) directly with plausible tools (exit closure, fences, permit parking). Clipping hit both sides roughly equally; format compliance was good on both. B's polished closing couldn't repair the empirical hole at the center of its mechanism.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's pressure Q2 ("name one site where geotag limits alone brought traffic below carrying capacity") plus A's Rebuttal 2 exposure of B's concession that the motion "reaches the selfie" — together collapsing B's tool into one both unproven and broader than advertised, while B's "rigged question" response read as evasion on the debate's central empirical ask.</best_rebuttal>
